name: Authority
description: People are more likely to trust or comply with a message when it is associated with perceived expertise, legitimacy, or high-status authority cues. In design, those cues can come from credentials, uniforms, institutional affiliation, verified badges, or expert endorsement.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to expert testimonials, clinician bylines, accreditation badges, verified-seller markers, security/compliance seals, and any flow that borrows trust from a visibly authoritative source.
prevalence_note: One of Cialdini's core persuasion principles, widely taught in marketing, trust, and conversion design.

findings.description: Across two field experiments, passersby complied more with arbitrary requests (picking up litter, giving a stranger a dime, moving away from a bus stop) from a confederate dressed as a security guard than from the same confederate dressed as a civilian or a milkman. The effect held even without the guard being able to observe compliance, suggesting the uniform's power came from perceived legitimacy rather than fear of surveillance — yet follow-up questionnaires found subjects did not consciously rate the guard as more powerful or legitimate than the other outfits, pointing to an automatic rather than deliberative response to the authority cue.
findings.source_title: The Social Power of a Uniform

findings.description: Synthesizing five decades of experimental persuasion research, high-credibility message sources are more persuasive than low-credibility sources as a robust main effect, but this advantage is not unconditional — it interacts with source, message, channel, receiver, and destination variables, and under certain moderating conditions a high-credibility source's edge shrinks or reverses. The review organizes these moderators and offers practitioner guidance on when to deploy a high- vs. low-credibility source.
findings.source_title: The Persuasiveness of Source Credibility: A Critical Review of Five Decades' Evidence

applications.title: Elena's Filipino Restaurant featuring a Guy Fieri TV endorsement
applications.description: Elena's Filipino Restaurant's website prominently features a celebrity endorsement -- chef Guy Fieri's coverage of the restaurant on his Food Network show -- alongside separate recognition from local food critics, using a well-known media personality's attention as a credibility signal.
applications.ethical_note: A real, verifiable media appearance (a specific TV show episode), not a fabricated or purchased endorsement claim as far as the source indicates -- a low-stakes, honest use of celebrity attention as social proof of quality.

applications.title: Fabric8Labs naming Mark Cuban among its investors
applications.description: Fabric8Labs lists Mark Cuban, a well-known venture capitalist, among its investors on its own site -- using a recognizable, high-profile name to lend credibility to the company by association.
applications.ethical_note: A real, presumably verifiable investment relationship rather than a fabricated affiliation -- authority-by-association used honestly, in a context (attracting business partners and customers to a startup) where investor credibility is a genuinely relevant signal.

applications.title: Milgram's obedience experiment: authority figures inducing harmful compliance
applications.description: Stanley Milgram's 1961-1963 obedience experiments had participants believe they were administering increasingly severe electric shocks to another person whenever a lab-coated experimenter (a perceived authority figure) instructed them to continue, despite the apparent victim's protests -- a majority of participants continued to the experiment's maximum, most severe level under the experimenter's authority alone.
applications.ethical_note: This is the canonical demonstration of authority bias producing genuinely harmful compliance -- participants believed they were causing real pain to another person because an authority figure told them to continue. Directly relevant to any interface or workflow that leans on perceived authority (official-looking badges, credentialed endorsements, system-generated recommendations framed as expert judgment) to override a user's own better judgment; the experiment itself is also a landmark case study in research ethics failures that shaped modern informed-consent standards.

applications.title: RocketLawyer.com stacking attorney credentials, press logos, and a security badge
applications.description: RocketLawyer.com combines several distinct authority signals at once -- attorney photos and staff credentials, logos from major news organizations that have covered the company, and a McAfee security badge -- layering expertise, media validation, and technical trust signals together.
applications.ethical_note: Authority signals here point to presumably real, checkable credentials (named attorneys, real press outlets, a known security certification) rather than vague or manufactured claims -- for a service category (legal advice) where verifying real expertise is itself in the user's own interest, this looks like the principle used in its clean form.
